Sets and subsets:
A set is a collection of objects where it is clear whether each object belongs to it. The objects are called elements. We write a ∈ A if a is in A, and a ∉ A if it is not. A set can be given by listing its elements in braces, such as {1, 2, 3}, or by a rule, such as {x | x is a natural number, x < 4}.

A is a subset of B, written A ⊆ B, if every element of A is also in B. The empty set ∅ is a subset of every set. A set with n elements has 2^n subsets, and 2^n - 1 of them are proper subsets.
Equal and unequal sets:
Two sets are equal if they have exactly the same elements. Order and repetition do not matter, so {1, 2, 3} = {3, 2, 1}. We write A = B if they are equal and A ≠ B if they are not.

A = B exactly when A ⊆ B and B ⊆ A. Equal sets have the same number of elements, n(A) = n(B), but sets with the same number of elements may still be unequal. To compare sets, write each one in roster form first. If a set contains an unknown, match the elements of the two sets to find it.
Union and intersection:
The union A ∪ B is the set of all elements that are in A, in B, or in both. The intersection A ∩ B is the set of elements that are in both A and B. If A ∩ B = ∅, the sets are called disjoint.

For finite sets, n(A ∪ B) = n(A) + n(B) - n(A ∩ B). Also A ∩ B ⊆ A ⊆ A ∪ B. If A ⊆ B, then A ∪ B = B and A ∩ B = A. Both operations are commutative, so the order of the two sets does not matter.
Complement of a set:
The universal set U contains all elements under discussion. The complement of A, written A', is the set of elements of U that are not in A. We have A ∪ A' = U, A ∩ A' = ∅, and n(A') = n(U) - n(A).

The difference A - B is the set of elements in A that are not in B, and A - B = A ∩ B'. De Morgan's laws say that (A ∪ B)' = A' ∩ B' and (A ∩ B)' = A' ∪ B'.
Finite and infinite sets:
A set is finite if counting its elements comes to an end. The number of elements is n(A), and n(∅) = 0. A set is infinite if the counting never ends, such as the natural numbers N = {1, 2, 3, ...}, the integers Z, or the even numbers.

A finite set with n elements has 2^n subsets. Every subset of a finite set is finite. A subset of an infinite set may be finite or infinite. The union of an infinite set with any set is infinite.
